title: How to remove an Airbnb review (and how to tell if yours qualifies)
summary: Airbnb removes reviews for exactly five reasons, and the dispute form gives you one reason and 2,500 characters to make the case. Here's what qualifies, what doesn't, how to build the case from the guest conversation you already have, and the structure that fits the form.
body_markdown:
**Every host eventually gets the review that isn't fair — the guest who trashed the place and then trashed you, the no-show who reviewed a stay that never happened, the one who threatened one star unless you refunded them. Airbnb does remove reviews like these. It does *not* remove an honest one-star from a guest who had a bad night, and no tool on earth changes that. The whole game is telling the two apart, then filing the case in the shape Airbnb's[Reviews Policy](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2673) and dispute form expect. Here's the playbook.**


## Key takeaways


- **Airbnb removes reviews for five reasons and nothing else:** retaliation, irrelevance, coercion, competitor abuse, and content-policy violations. "It's unfair" is not on the list.
- **Two of the five are provable from records** — retaliation and irrelevance — which is why they're the ones worth filing. The rest need a smoking gun in writing.
- **You file it yourself, in your Airbnb dashboard:** pick one reason, write up to 2,500 characters, attach files. Airbnb usually answers within 48 hours, and you get at most two tries per review.
- **The guest conversation is the evidence.** Timestamped messages that contradict the review, or that show a rule being enforced right before it landed, win disputes. Feelings don't.
- **When it doesn't qualify, respond publicly instead.** Fewer than 1 in 1,000 reviews gets a host response, so a calm reply under a bad review does more for your next booking than the dispute ever would.


## Where we're coming from


We run our own portfolio on ProhostAI — a[4.99 rating across more than 3,000 reviews](https://prohost.ai/about) — so we've been on the receiving end of the unfair review, and we've filed the dispute. Before ProhostAI, I spent years on Airbnb's hosting team, close enough to the review system to know that the people ruling on disputes are reading for policy, not sympathy. That's the lens for everything below: what would a reviewer with the policy open in one tab and your submission in the other actually need to see?


## What Airbnb will and won't remove


Airbnb's starting position is that a review is the guest's honest account of the stay. In the policy's own words, a review "won't be removed solely due to disagreement with the star rating," and subjective opinions stay up because "the guest's perspective may provide helpful information." Roughly[five in six Airbnb reviews are already 5 stars](https://www.prohost.ai/blog/how-to-get-more-5-star-reviews) , so the angry ones are rare — but when one lands, it's the exception Airbnb is designed to protect, not the one it's designed to remove.


What it *will* remove is a review that breaks the policy, and the dispute form lists the five grounds it considers:


1. **It's retaliatory.** Left in retaliation for a policy or rule being enforced — in Airbnb's wording, users "may not write reviews to retaliate against another user for enforcing an Airbnb policy." The classic sequence: you reported damage, declined an out-of-policy refund, or refused the extra guests, and the review followed. One caveat straight from the policy: a review "discussing the facts or legitimacy of a Resolution Center or AirCover claim isn't automatically considered retaliatory." The claim isn't the case. The sequence and the evidence are.
2. **It's irrelevant.** The review says nothing about the reservation, or the guest never arrived. The policy is explicit: "if a guest never arrived for their reservation or chose to cancel due to circumstances unrelated to the offering they booked, their review will be considered irrelevant." A review that isn't based on a real reservation at all is treated as fake and comes down for the same reason.
3. **It involves pressure or coercion.** The review was extorted, incentivized, or written under threat. The policy bars using a review to "extort, incentivize, or pressure" the other party, and says reviews "may not be provided or withheld in exchange for something of value." A guest who put "refund me or it's one star" in writing is the textbook case.
4. **It was posted by a competitor.** Someone affiliated with, or competing against, your listing.
5. **It doesn't follow the Content Policy.** Discriminatory language, your private information, or other content violations.


Airbnb adds that it "will start with your selection but may also consider other reasons," so pick the strongest fit and let the details carry the rest.


## The two you can actually prove


Retaliation and irrelevance are the reasons worth your time, because both can be *shown* from records rather than *argued* from opinion.


**Retaliation is a sequence.** A rule was enforced, then the review arrived. If your thread shows you declining a refund on Tuesday and a one-star review lands Wednesday with no mention of the refund, that sequence is your case. The more concrete the enforcement, the better: the house-rules screenshot, the damage report you filed, the extra-guest message you sent.


**Irrelevance is usually a no-show.** The reservation record shows no check-in, the guidebook was never opened, the lock never turned, and the review describes a stay that didn't happen. Reservation timelines beat opinions every time.


**Coercion is provable when it's in writing.** "Refund me or I'll leave one star" in the Airbnb thread is as strong as evidence gets. A threat made by phone is close to unprovable — which is one more reason to keep every guest conversation on the platform.


## Filing the dispute


The form lives in your Airbnb host dashboard — reach it from the review itself or from Airbnb's["Request to remove a review"](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/3582) help page — and it's two screens.


**Screen one: "Why should this review be removed?"** One radio button, the five reasons above.


**Screen two: "Can you tell us more?"** A free-text box capped at 2,500 characters, plus "Upload photos or files." Airbnb's own note on the upload: don't include sensitive info like credit card numbers.


Airbnb says it usually responds within 48 hours. You can request removal of the same review up to two times, and if it's denied you're offered a way to contact Airbnb if you believe there's been a mistake. That second request is a narrow door, not an appeal — so the first submission is the one that has to be complete.


## Writing the 2,500 characters


Most disputes fail in one of two ways: they argue the review is *wrong* instead of showing it *violates policy* , or they burn the space on an emotional preamble and run out before the evidence. The details box is a brief, not a complaint. The structure we use:


1. **One sentence naming the ground.** "This review is retaliatory: it was posted within 24 hours of my declining a refund request that fell outside the cancellation policy."
2. **The timeline, with timestamps.** Three to five lines — booking date, the enforcement event, the review date.
3. **The contradictions, quoted.** For each claim in the review, the guest's own message that contradicts it, with date and time. "Review says the apartment was 'filthy on arrival.' Guest message, 14 Aug 15:42: 'Place looks great, thanks for the welcome basket.'"
4. **What's attached.** One line listing the files.
5. **The ask.** One sentence: "I request removal under the Reviews Policy on the grounds above."


No adjectives about the guest, nothing about how the review made you feel, nothing about what the rating does to your business. The reviewer is reading for policy; everything else is noise that costs characters.


## What to upload


The upload is optional on the form and decisive in practice. In rough order of weight:


- **Message excerpts with timestamps.** Screenshots or a PDF export of the exact exchanges you quoted, so the reviewer can verify without hunting through the thread.
- **The reservation timeline.** Booking, check-in, checkout, any cancellation. For a no-show this *is* the case.
- **The rule that was enforced.** A screenshot of your house rules or cancellation policy as the guest saw them at booking.
- **Photos, where relevant.** Damage photos for a retaliation case built on a damage claim; timestamped turnover photos for a cleanliness dispute.


Keep private data out — nothing about the guest beyond what they wrote to you, and no payment or ID details for anyone.


## When the review doesn't qualify


Here's the uncomfortable part. Most negative reviews are a guest's honest opinion, and filing a dispute on one of those does nothing except spend your credibility with Airbnb for the next one that matters. Two better moves:


**Respond publicly.** In our data, fewer than 1 in 1,000 reviews gets a host response — almost nobody does it. A short, specific, gracious reply sits directly under the review and is read by every future guest who scrolls that far, which is far more people than will ever weigh the review on its own. Acknowledge the point, say what changed, thank them for the stay. Never argue. A calm response next to an angry review wins the reader every time.


**Fix the thing.** If three reviews mention the same shower, the shower is the problem. Reviews are the cheapest maintenance report you'll ever get.

## Frequently asked questions


**How long do I have to dispute a review?** Airbnb says a review you received can be disputed at any time. File as soon as it appears anyway — recent context is easier to verify, and a stale dispute reads as an afterthought.


**Can I get a review removed for being untrue?** Only if the untruth falls under one of the five reasons. A false claim about the stay is treated as the guest's opinion unless it's irrelevant, retaliatory, coerced, competitive, or a content violation. Contradicting evidence *strengthens* a retaliation or coercion case, but "it's not true" alone is not a ground.


**Will disputing a review hurt my account?** Not on its own. Filing weak disputes repeatedly is a different matter — which is why this post spends so long on whether a review qualifies before how to file.


**Can I edit or delete my own review of the guest?** You can't edit it, but you can remove a review you wrote for up to 30 days from the date it was published. After that it stays.


**What if the review argues about a Resolution Center or AirCover claim?** That alone doesn't make it retaliatory — Airbnb's policy says so explicitly. What makes the case is showing the review was written *because* you enforced a policy, with the timeline to prove it. A review that is only about the claim and says nothing about the stay can also be argued as irrelevant.


## The takeaway


Removing an Airbnb review isn't about how wrong it is; it's about whether it breaks one of five rules, and whether you can show that from the record. Retaliation and no-shows are provable. Almost everything else is a public response, not a dispute. Keep the conversation on the platform, keep the timeline, write the brief for a reviewer reading for policy — and for the 999 in 1,000 reviews that don't need any of this, make sure every one of them gets a reply.
